description:
Team Infonic is a group of passionate students driven by curiosity, creativity, and technology. We combine our skills in coding, research, design, and problem-solving to tackle real-world challenges.

At NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to turn open data and innovative ideas into meaningful, practical solutions while learning, collaborating, and pushing the boundaries of what we can build together.

details:
What it does. On Earth, flames are teardrop-shaped because gravity drives buoyant convection. In freefall, buoyancy disappears, flames become dim, blue and spherical, and they can spread in unexpected ways. IGNIS brings NASA microgravity combustion knowledge into one connected website. A person can explore the research, simulate flames, check flammability and consult a safety assistant without searching through scattered reports.

How it works. The platform has these modules:

  • Data Visualisation Network: an interactive graph linking NASA combustion experiments, from Skylab to modern Saffire and ACME flights.
  • PSI Sentence Search: plain-language search over NASA PSI research records that returns the exact sentences about thresholds, extinction and mission data.
  • PSI & NTRS Vault: curated NASA flight investigations with NTRS citations.
  • Flame Simulator: a 3D chamber that shows flame shape and colour for Earth, Moon, Mars and ISS gravity and for Saffire-style cabin atmospheres.
  • Flammability Predictor: an in-browser machine-learning model calibrated on 48 verified NASA PSI test runs. It includes a 2D phase-space map and CSV export.
  • Hardware Explorer: spaceflight combustion hardware and its Earth spin-offs.
  • Station Guardian: a 3D digital twin of the station with blast, decompression and fire scenarios. Wait for 3-4 minutes to load full simulation
  • Aether-SI: a conversational fire-safety assistant grounded in the PSI records.

Benefits and impact. The project helps students, researchers and mission-safety teams understand how fire behaves in spacecraft. It shows why oxygen level, airflow and pressure matter for crew safety. Data that was spread across many documents becomes searchable, visual and interactive. The same ideas also support Earth fire-safety education.

Tools and technologies. We used React, TypeScript, Vite, Node.js and Express for the web apps and server. Three.js drives the 3D simulators, and HTML, CSS and JavaScript power the research pages. Aether-SI uses a Google Gemini model. The data comes from public NASA sources (PSI, NTRS and flight experiment reports). The platform is hosted on Render.

What is creative. We combined research search, simulation, prediction and emergency scenarios into one mission-control style website instead of building separate tools. The simulator’s range check shows when a result falls outside NASA’s tested conditions, so users can see what is measured and what is estimated.

Factors we considered. We labelled estimates versus NASA-sourced values and added guardrails so the tools do not overclaim. The flame rendering is illustrative and interpolated between known conditions, and the predictor is trained on a small dataset. IGNIS is an educational and practically valuable prototype built on public data .
dataRefs: NASA ACME (Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments)
NTRS: Cold Atom Laboratory on the ISS
